also: treat the place as your own

terms.gloss: eat, drink, please yourself: the host’s welcome
terms.grammar: imperatives of edō, bibō, and obsequor (with the dative animō)
evidence: Plaut. Mil. 677: ēs, bibe, animō obsequere mēcum atque onerā tē hilaritūdine
terms.comment: What Plautus’s generous host says to the young man staying in his house: eat, drink, and indulge yourself with me. It is the nearest thing to “make yourself at home” we have found in the authors. Cicero says of a host who treated him so apud eum ego sīc … fuī … tamquam domī meae, “at his house I was as if in my own home”; see the examples. For “make yourselves comfortable”, see “comfortable”.

phrases.latin: Ēs, bibe, animō obsequere mēcum atque onerā tē hilaritūdine.
phrases.english: Eat, drink, enjoy yourself with me, and load yourself up with good cheer.

phrases.latin: Apud eum ego sīc Ephesī fuī, quotiēscumque fuī, tamquam domī meae.
phrases.english: Whenever I was in Ephesus I stayed at his house as if it were my own home.

phrases.latin: Tuam esse hanc domum putā: sūme quod vīs.
phrases.english: Make yourself at home: help yourself to whatever you like.

phrases.latin: Cōnsīde, quaesō; ēs, bibe, ut libet.
phrases.english: Do sit down; eat and drink as you like.

sources: Lewis & Short: edo · Lewis & Short: bibo · Lewis & Short: obsequor · Lewis & Short: tamquam
